newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chirac impressed by Yeltsin, optimistic on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Chirac impressed by Yeltsin, optimistic on NATO.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Sunday he was impressed by Boris Yeltsin's recovery from pneumonia and declared after talks he was optimistic Russia and NATO could reach accord on the alliance's eastward expansion.

Chirac was speaking at Moscow's Vnukovo-2 airport after an afternoon of talks with Yeltsin at his Novo-Ogaryovo country residence. The meeting marked the Russian president's first foray onto the world stage since his treatment for pneumonia.
"I was impressed by the speed of his recovery," Chirac said.

"I found him as always extraordinarily well informed about all the problems of the world which we discussed together and very tough in the defence of Russia's interests, which is entirely legitimate."
A scheduled two-hour meeting was extended by an hour.

Earlier in the day Yeltsin, bundled in a heavy black coat and fur hat, had looked in good humour when greeting Chirac on the snow-swept forecourt of Novo-Ogaryova. He walked a little stiffly but seemed alert and his voice was clear and steady, creating an altogether more vigorous impression than on edited television film broadcast earlier in the week.
Chirac brought the Russian president a parcel tied with a white ribbon for his 66th birthday on Saturday.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, who had heart surgery in November and faces opposition charges he is too ill to govern, was "highly satisfied" with the talks.
"(Yeltsin said that) on many issues, especially European issues, the positions of Russia and France coincide," he said.
Russia objects to NATO plans for eastward expansion, insisting the incorporation of former Moscow allies in the Western grouping would undermine Russian security.

Chirac said that NATO and Russia should show respect for each other in the approach to a Madrid alliance summit that is expected to issue the first invitations to former Warsaw Pact countries to join the grouping. They should also be flexible.
"If these conditions are met, I think -- and this is my personal impression -- that an agreement can be reached before the ((July) Madrid summit."
He said France had no strong feelings on whether an agreement should take the form of a legally binding charter or an informal declaration.

Since NATO made clear that Russia's objections would not stop its expansion, Moscow appears to have switched to negotiating a deal which would keep the alliance's military structures away from its borders.
Government officials say Russia is seeking a binding document rather than a political declaration.
They say that in an ideal world this document should include a promise not to deploy nuclear forces, heavy weapons and troops belonging to other NATO states on the territory of new members.
Moscow is clearly looking for support from within NATO, especially from some of its European members who seek to take over some alliance command functions from the United States.
Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.

The Russian president spent his birthday on Saturday quietly with his family. He was joined in the evening by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, just back from an economic summit in Switzerland, and chief aide Anatoly Chubais.
Yeltsin's wife, Naina, said he was recovering well.

"Doctors say that if he were just a normal man he should have stayed in hospital...It takes longer to recover if you work at the same time." His condition, she said, allowed him more time to watch television and to think.
"Now he has more time to...weigh things," she said in a television interview. His daughter, Tatyana, said the family had bought the president a quilted jacket as a present.
